input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

But the owner said the boxes had belonged to a local radio engineer named Martin Vale. I had never heard of him before, and the shop was narrow enough that two people had to turn sideways to pass each other. The front windows were fogged from the rain, and a little brass bell over the door kept ringing whenever someone came in. I got there on Sunday morning, just after ten, and there were already six people waiting by the counter. The owner had put a paper cup of coffee beside the register and told everyone the records would be brought out one crate at a time, so nobody had to crowd around the back room.

I had been collecting for about eight years by then, mostly used jazz and soul records, and I had learned not to judge a collection from the first few sleeves. The first crate had water marks on the bottom and smelled a little like a basement, but the records themselves were clean enough. There were labels I knew from Chicago and Detroit and a few small local pressings with plain white covers. One sleeve had a note in blue pencil that said, “Play side two after midnight,” and another had a radio station call sign written near the opening. I asked whether Martin had worked at the station, and the owner said yes, he had repaired turntables and reel-to-reel machines there through the late seventies. That was the first detail that made the sale feel like more than a lucky shelf of records.

1. The first thing I picked up for myself was a 1974 pressing of a live quartet set recorded in a small university hall. The cover was soft at the corners, and someone had written a date inside in a careful block hand: November 3, 1978. I recognized the pianist but not the drummer, and the track list included a piece with a title I had only seen once in an old club listing. I put it back because the price tag said forty dollars, and then I took it out again when the owner mentioned that the original inner sleeve was still there. I asked if he would hold it while I looked through the next box, and he said sure, but only until noon because another buyer had called about the same pressing.

The second crate was harder to sort through, since the labels were mixed and several albums had been filed into the wrong jackets. I found two copies of the same folk record: one was a later reissue, and the other had a small pressing plant mark near the center hole. There were also three spoken-word records from a community theater project and a holiday album with a cracked corner but no scratches on the playing surface. I remember thinking that the damaged cover might still be worth taking home, but I was trying not to buy things just because they had an interesting story. I used my phone flashlight to check the grooves, and the shop owner laughed and said the old engineer would have approved of that level of caution.

2. By eleven thirty, the rain had stopped, and the room felt warmer because the door kept opening. I had set aside four records and was trying to decide which one to return to the crate: first, the live quartet, because it was the most expensive; second, a local blues single with a plain sleeve; third, an orchestral record that had a handwritten note about a broadcast date; and fourth, a small label compilation that I already knew from a friend. I said, “Maybe the blues single,” but I meant the quartet and corrected myself before the owner reached for the wrong one. He put the quartet behind the counter and told me I could listen to it on the shop turntable if I wanted.

The listening station was tucked beside a stack of repair manuals, and the speakers were small but clear. I used the shop’s headphones and played the opening of the first side. There was a soft tick for a few seconds, and then the piano came in with a warm sound that felt close without being loud. The drummer used brushes, and the bass was slightly quieter than I expected, but the recording had a steady room sound that made me want to hear the whole set. I stopped after the first track because the shop had become busy and someone was waiting to use the turntable. While I put the record away, I noticed a second note in the sleeve that listed the names of the musicians and a phone number with the last two digits smudged.

I bought the quartet and the blues single and left the other two records for another day. The total was fifty-three dollars, including tax, and the owner wrapped the jackets in brown paper instead of giving me a plastic bag. Outside, I sat on a low stone wall and checked that the paper had not torn in the rain. I called my partner to say I would be home later than planned and told them about the radio engineer and the pencil notes. They asked if I had bought anything we could actually play at dinner, and I said the blues single was probably the better choice for that. On the drive home, I kept the records upright in the passenger footwell and took the slower road because the main street had a line of road work cones.

When I got home, I cleaned both records with the brush I use for new arrivals and played the blues single first. It had a dry little guitar sound and a singer who left a breath between every line. The quartet took longer because I checked the labels and the inner sleeve before putting it on. The date in the cover turned out to be a week after the hall had hosted a campus fundraiser, and I wondered if the set had been made for the station’s overnight program, but I could not tell from the notes alone. A month later, the owner messaged me that he had found another box of Martin’s records and asked whether I wanted first look.
